extracted.intended_audience: citizens/voters and constitutional designers considering the proposed U.S. Constitution; legislators and framers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating constitutional design with emphasis on the distribution of legislative, executive, and judicial powers and the practical mechanisms (checks, controls, and conventions) needed to prevent usurpation and preserve liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia versus standing army (relative military sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest number to which, according to the best computation, a standing army can be carried in any country, does not exceed one hundredth part of the whole number of souls; or one twenty-fifth part of the number able to bear arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the potential size of a regular standing army (estimated at 1/100 of population or ~1/25 of those able to bear arms) with militia strength (in the U.S. example near half a million). Evaluate whether militia—officered by locally chosen men, attached to local governments, and fighting for local liberties—provides a realistic defense against a federal standing army. Consider Americans' advantage of being armed and the role of subordinate governments in organizing and directing force; weigh historical examples of successful resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of subordinate (state/local) governments as a barrier to ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of subordinate governments, to which the people are attached, and by which the militia officers are appointed, forms a barrier against the enterprises of ambition, more insurmountable than any which a simple government of any form can admit of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether local/state governments chosen by the people can collect popular support, appoint militia officers trusted by citizens, and thereby resist central usurpation. Consider the assertion that local governments plus an armed citizen militia could overturn tyrannical thrones—use as a criterion for preventing centralized tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must be dependent on the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the mode in which the federal government is to be constructed will render it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge constitutional structures by whether they ensure the federal government's dependence on popular will. If dependent, the federal government will be restrained from schemes against constituents; if not, it won't possess public confidence and state governments supported by the people can defeat federal usurpation. Use this as a test for legitimacy and practical restraining power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid accumulation of all powers in same hands (definition of tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands ... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate any constitutional plan by whether it permits one person or body (single, few, or many) to exercise the whole of multiple departments' powers. If so, treat the plan as liable to tyranny. Use this as a fundamental negative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper interpretation of Montesquieu's maxim (whole vs partial blending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's meaning ... can amount to no more than this, that where the WHOLE power of one department is exercised by the same hands which possess the WHOLE power of another department, the fundamental principles of a free constitution are subverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Montesquieu's prohibition narrowly: full fusion of entire departments is the danger, whereas partial agency, checks, or interconnection (as in the British constitution) are compatible with liberty. Use historical examples (British Constitution features) to distinguish permissible inter-department relations from unconstitutional consolidations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation only 'as the nature of a free government will admit' (practical mixed functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT; OR AS IS CONSISTENT WITH THAT CHAIN OF CONNECTION THAT BINDS THE WHOLE FABRIC OF THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE INDISSOLUBLE BOND OF UNITY AND AMITY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that absolute, total separation is impracticable; evaluate constitutions by whether they preserve essential separation to the extent compatible with unity and functioning government. Examine specific state constitutional arrangements (appointments, impeachment jurisdiction, ex officio roles) to see whether the mixing is within acceptable practical bounds or constitutes harmful consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departments should have constitutional control over each other (checks and balances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless these departments be so far connected and blended as to give to each a constitutional control over the others, the degree of separation which the maxim requires ... can never in practice be duly maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require mutual constitutional controls (vetoes, appointment powers, impeachment/removal, appellate jurisdiction, legislative oversight) so each branch can check encroachments by others. Evaluate whether the design provides effective, practicable countervailing powers rather than only theoretical separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere demarcation on parchment is insufficient; need practical securities
rubrics_metrics.description: Will it be sufficient to mark, with precision, the boundaries of these departments, in the constitution of the government, and to trust to these parchment barriers against the encroaching spirit of power? ... a mere demarcation on parchment of the constitutional limits ... is not a sufficient guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize constitutional text for enforceable mechanisms and institutional arrangements that realize separation in practice. Use empirical evidence (state experience, councils of censors, records) to test whether textual limits have practical force. Favor institutional features that create durable, operational restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate legislative encroachment and design safeguards accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative department is everywhere extending the sphere of its activity, and drawing all power into its impetuous vortex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing risks, treat the legislature as the likeliest source of encroachment because of extensive, ill-defined powers and control over public purse. Ensure specific safeguards (procedural, institutional, independent judiciary salaries/tenure, executive independence) to protect weaker departments from legislative usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a constitutional road of appeal to the people (convention) for extraordinary corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: That whenever any two of the three branches of government shall concur in opinion, each by the voices of two thirds of their whole number, that a convention is necessary for altering the constitution, or CORRECTING BREACHES OF IT, a convention shall be called for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a mechanism for calling a constitutional convention as a last-resort remedy for breaches or major alterations; treat it as consonant with republican theory because ultimate authority rests with the people. However, evaluate scope and thresholds carefully to avoid misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on frequent appeals to the people (risks of conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: As every appeal to the people would carry an implication of some defect in the government, frequent appeals would, in a great measure, deprive the government of that veneration which time bestows on every thing ... The danger of disturbing the public tranquillity by interesting too strongly the public passions, is a still more serious objection against a frequent reference of constitutional questions to the decision of the whole society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on conventions as an ordinary remedial device. Assess whether thresholds and limitations prevent overuse—frequent recourse undermines stability, invites passion, and may fail to preserve constitutional equilibrium. Use conventions only for rare, great occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of fusing judiciary with legislative or executive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or body of magistrates ... Were the power of judging joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control, for THE JUDGE would then be THE LEGISLATOR. Were it joined to the executive power, THE JUDGE might behave with all the violence of AN OPPRESSOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any institutional arrangement that makes judges also legislators or executives as jeopardizing individual rights. Evaluate appointment/removal mechanisms, participation of judges in legislative councils, or executive roles to ensure the judiciary retains impartial adjudicative function distinct from making or executing law.
